title: Ice for Prairie Avenue
premise: Play the iceman's young helper on a Monday morning in October 1904: find the way in at 1800 Prairie Avenue, where the family has one door and the ice another, and decide whether to wait for the kitchen or run ahead.

opening.text:
JAUNT: ICE FOR PRAIRIE AVENUE. A Monday morning in October 1904, and you are thirteen, riding the back of an ice wagon down Prairie Avenue. The iceman lifts the blocks; you do everything else, and you are paid accordingly. Your job this morning is to find the way in at houses built so that people like you are never seen coming in.

Every family here has a door of its own. The ice has another, and so do the cook, the maids and the boy from the wagon. The first house is the granite one at the corner of Eighteenth Street. Find your door before the ice drips. The houses and the people in them are real; the iceman's helper is you.

stops.text: Here at the corner of Prairie Avenue and Eighteenth Street, John Glessner built his house diagonally opposite Pullman's mansion and across the street from W. W. Kimball's smaller French chateau. Its outside walls are Wellesley granite, lined with hollow brick, so there is no place for a mouse to live, and no easy way for anyone else either. Passers-by remark on the narrow slots of windows along Eighteenth Street; the generous windows face the private courtyard. From the street it is a fortress, and it means to be one.
stops.narrative: Which way in for the ice?

choices.label: Knock at the front door
choices.consequence: It is the grandest door on the corner.

choices.label: Round by the alley
choices.consequence: A big house must have a back way somewhere.

stops.text: The door on Prairie Avenue is the family's, and not one you will ever use. Henry Hobson Richardson designed this house, his last work, and the Glessners have slept here since 1 December 1887. It is Monday: every Monday from October to May Mrs. Glessner's Reading Class meets for two hours in the library, by invitation only, the ladies sewing while a professional reader reads to them. Their carriages will draw up here soon, and a boy with dripping ice is the last thing this doorstep is for. An underpass runs beside you into the courtyard. Go round.

Round the back, off the alley, are the courtyard gates. Through them, on 1 December 1887, the Glessners moved every belonging they had 'before our neighbors suspected even that we were about to move', and lit the new hearth that night with fire carried from the old house. The plan let even its owners move in unseen. Above the court the dovecotes hold nearly sixty doves, and their eggs go to the family's table. Even here the ice stops short: the service entrance is round on Eighteenth Street.
stops.narrative: The back way in, but not for ice.

stops.text: Under the great arch on Eighteenth Street is the service entrance, with a separate address, 35 Eighteenth Street, so the staff do not even share the family's number. A small corridor runs to the kitchen; its window sits in the arch. The ice never comes indoors: it goes through a half-door into the cold closet, and the iceman never sets foot inside. An annunciator tells the kitchen which room has rung, and the staff eat at about three so the kitchen can turn to the family's dinner. There is one cook, Mattie Williamson, since 1892, when Mrs. Glessner dismissed her seventh cook in seven weeks.
stops.narrative: Wait for the kitchen, or run ahead?

choices.label: Wait for the kitchen
choices.consequence: You will know how much ice to bring next time; the wagon waits at the stable doors.

choices.label: Run ahead
choices.consequence: You will find the Kimballs' back way before the wagon gets there.

stops.text: The wagon waits by the stable's carriage doorway on Eighteenth Street, where the iceman can water his horse. Six stalls, room for as many carriages, all of it white glazed brick, and the furnace room underneath so that the dust, dirt and noise of coal and ashes never reach the family. Somebody shovels that coal. Who drives for the Glessners now is not recorded: their coachman of twenty-four years left in 1902. In two years the horses will go for motor cars, and the wall between stable and carriage house will come down.

Across Prairie Avenue at 1801 is W. W. Kimball's house, built in 1890 to Solon S. Beman's design in the French Chateauesque style, a very steep slate roof and a round tower under a slate cone. Kimball began in Chicago in 1857, 'beginning with only four pianos'; by 1881 his factory was 'churning out around 100 pianos and organs every week'. He has two months to live: he 'died at his home in Chicago on December 16, 1904'. The back way in will be just as hard to find.
stops.narrative: The next house on the round.

legs.note: A few steps south along the Prairie Avenue front to the door.
legs.story: The grandest door on the corner, then.

legs.note: West along Eighteenth Street past the stable, and round into the alley to the courtyard gates.
legs.story: Every big house has a back way, if you can find it.

legs.note: Back to the corner and west along Eighteenth Street to the great arch.
legs.story: Round the corner, before the ice drips any more.

legs.note: Out of the alley and east along Eighteenth Street to the great arch.
A little way west along Eighteenth Street to the carriage doorway.
East to the corner and across Prairie Avenue.
legs.story: Across the avenue at a run.

endings.text: The back way first, the kitchen's order taken, the horse watered: the iceman says you will do, which is as near to praise as you will get. Next Monday you will go round by the alley without being told. The kitchen will learn your face at the half-door; upstairs, nobody ever will.

You found the Glessners' back way on your own, and you are across Prairie Avenue ahead of the wagon, hunting for the Kimballs'. The iceman will not say he is pleased. Every house on this street has a door for the family and another for everything that serves it, and you are learning them one alley at a time.

You learned the hard way that the big door on Prairie Avenue is not for the likes of you, but you learned it before the Reading Class arrived. The kitchen's order is in your pocket and the horse is watered. Next Monday you go round by Eighteenth Street, and you never knock at the front again.

Two lessons before ten o'clock: the front door is the family's, and a wagon waits for nobody. You are across Prairie Avenue looking for the Kimballs' back way while the iceman whistles for you. Tomorrow the round starts again, and the doors on this street will not get any easier to find.

keepsake.title: The Ice Round
keepsake.text: A fictional card of one morning's ice round on Prairie Avenue in October 1904: which door you tried first and where you went next. No real delivery, order or helper is written on it.

evidence.text: Glessner built at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue, diagonally opposite Pullman's mansion and across the street from W. W. Kimball's smaller French chateau.
evidence.locator: Data page 3, Part I.B.

evidence.text: The outside walls on the streets are of Wellesley granite, and all walls are lined with hollow brick, to which the plastering is attached without laths, so there is no place for mice behind the plastering.
evidence.locator: HABS data page 13.

evidence.text: Passers-by remarked on the narrow windows in the north side along 18th Street, just enough to light the narrow corridors, not realizing that on the courtyard side Richardson had put generous windows.
evidence.locator: HABS data page 15.

evidence.text: Henry Hobson Richardson designed the house; Glessner calls it his last work.
evidence.locator: HABS data page 2 (architect); Story of a House, HABS data page 13 ('It was his last work').

evidence.text: The family slept in the house for the first time on the night of 1 December 1887.
evidence.locator: HABS data page 9.

evidence.text: In 1893 William Rainey Harper, president of the University of Chicago, asked Frances Glessner for advice on how to introduce faculty wives to women of the city. The result was her Monday Morning Reading Class, which met for two hours in the library of the house every Monday from October to May. During the first hour the women sewed and listened to a professional reader; during the second there was lighter reading or a lecture. Membership was by invitation only, and the class continued until 1930.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: An underpass on the east (Prairie Avenue) front leads under the house to the courtyard.
evidence.locator: HABS data page 2 (Part I.A.6, 'the door of the underpass on the east facade'); drawings sheet 2, the first-floor plan.

evidence.text: On 1 December 1887 the family moved all their belongings in through the courtyard entrance from the alley before the neighbours suspected they were moving, and lit the new hearth with fire carried from the old house at Washington and Morgan Streets; they were in 'before our neighbors suspected even that we were about to move'.
evidence.locator: HABS data pages 8-9.

evidence.text: Doves in the dovecotes, which held nearly sixty, gave the family eggs.
evidence.locator: The post.

evidence.text: The service entrance is through the great arch on Eighteenth Street to a small corridor and the kitchen.
evidence.locator: Story of a House, HABS data page 15; drawings sheet 5, the 18th Street entrance arch.

evidence.text: The servants had their own address, 35 Eighteenth Street (renumbered 227 E. 18th Street in 1909), and separate entrances, the women's set within the great arch.
evidence.locator: The post.

evidence.text: The women servants' entrance is set within the great arch on Eighteenth Street, and the kitchen window sits within the arch.
evidence.locator: The post, on George Glessner's photograph of about 1890.

evidence.text: The servants ate their own dinner at about three o'clock, so that the kitchen could turn to the family's dinner afterwards; an annunciator in the kitchen showed which room had rung, and the iceman delivered ice through a half-door into the cold closet.
evidence.locator: The post's account of the kitchen's routines.

evidence.text: The Glessners only ever had one cook at a time; Kate Ryan, whom the census of 1 June 1900 found cooking for the house, was the temporary summer cook in Chicago while Mattie Williamson was in New Hampshire with the family.
evidence.locator: The owner's message of 13 November 2026, relaying Bill Tyre of Glessner House.

evidence.text: In February 1892, hired as a maid, Mattie Williamson became the cook after Frances Glessner dismissed her seventh cook in seven weeks; the cooks had struggled with a new gas stove. Frances wrote: 'Mattie Williamson is going to try my cooking. I shall have her taught.'
evidence.locator: The post, quoting Frances Glessner's journal for February 1892.

evidence.text: Mattie Williamson left in 1912 to marry William Prescott in Los Angeles; Frances Glessner later wrote to her son that Mattie was 'one of the finest people that ever lived.'
evidence.locator: The post's account of her marriage and death.

evidence.text: The stable's carriage doorway opens on Eighteenth Street.
evidence.locator: Sheets 2 and 5: the 18th Street carriage doorway.

evidence.text: The stable had six stalls for horses, and the carriage house could hold as many carriages.
evidence.locator: The post's account of the coach house and stable.

evidence.text: The carriage house and stables are of white glazed brick, and the house is heated from the furnace room under them, keeping the dust and dirt and noise of coal and ashes out of the house.
evidence.locator: Story of a House, HABS data page 13; HABS data page 22.

evidence.text: Charles Nelson, an immigrant from Sweden, was the Glessners' coachman from 1878 until 1902, so he was no longer in their service in 1904; who drove for them from 1902 is not recorded in the sources read.
evidence.locator: Page 3, 'Secrets of Glessner House, Part 19: The Coachman'.

evidence.text: In 1906 the Glessners changed to automobiles, and the wall between the stable and the carriage house was taken down.
evidence.locator: The post's account of the coach house and stable.

evidence.text: William W. Kimball Residence. Built 1890; Solon S. Beman, architect. Built for the prominent Chicago piano and organ manufacturer in the French Chateauesque style.
evidence.locator: The 1801 S. Prairie Avenue entry.

evidence.text: J. W. Taylor's photograph of about 1895 shows a very steep slate roof over the main block and a round tower on the 18th Street flank under a slate cone.
evidence.locator: The whole print, from the north-west across 18th Street and Prairie Avenue.

evidence.text: Kimball founded his piano business in Chicago in 1857, 'beginning with only four pianos'; in 1881 he opened his own factory 'churning out around 100 pianos and organs every week'; he 'died at his home in Chicago on December 16, 1904'.
evidence.locator: The biography: Chicago, the factory, his death.

evidence.text: The six stops are exterior stands round 1800 Prairie Avenue and on the avenue at Kimball's corner, the stands the published Glessner jaunts use. The ice's half-door is the house's own, but where along the service side it opens is not stated, so no stop claims its spot, and no interior is entered.
evidence.reasoning: The half-door into the cold closet is the museum's account of the kitchen's routines; the HABS drawings place the great arch, the underpass and the stable's carriage doorway on Eighteenth Street, which is where the stands stand. The stop at the arch speaks of the service entrance and the kitchen behind it, and of the half-door without placing it.

evidence.text: The iceman's helper the visitor plays, their age, the iceman, his wagon and horse, the Monday in October 1904, the round and its order, the doors tried, the kitchen's order and the watering of the horse, the choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and The Ice Round keepsake are invented connective narrative. No ice delivery on a day in 1904 is asserted and no named person is met or speaks; the Reading Class's Monday meetings are attested, its carriages on this morning are not.
